definition: Names a specific user, customer or audience, like "freelance designers" or "busy parents". "Users" or "people" alone is no.
States the problem or pain the work solves, like "people forget utility changes". Describing only the feature is no.
Says how to tell the product worked: a number, target or outcome, like "cut repeat tickets by 20%" or "60% completion". "Make it good" is no.

Lists concrete conditions the finished work must meet to count as done, like "Done means a user can create an invoice" or "search returns a useful article for 8 of 10 queries". A business target like "signup rate above 5%" is a success metric, not acceptance criteria. Saying what to skip is scope, not acceptance.
Says what to leave out, skip or keep for later, or limits the first version, like "MVP excludes payments" or "don't add social sharing yet".
Splits the work into ordered steps or phases, like "first add dates, then schedule reminders". A list of features is not steps.
Gives examples, references, existing material or the current state to build on, like "use the existing docs" or "keep the current export format".
Only for follow-ups that change something that already exists. yes if it says exactly what is wrong and what to change. notApplicable if the prompt starts something new.
Asks for tests or a way to check the result, like "test overdue invoices" or "add a way to verify search quality".
Mentions cost, budget, speed, performance, a deadline or another limit the work must respect, like "loads in under 2 seconds" or "launch next month".
Mentions errors, empty states, invalid input or other edge cases to handle, like "check the empty-data state".
Names a technology, platform, library, data store or format to use or keep, like "Use React and local storage" or "keep it mobile-first".
Bad habit. Asks for a feature or product with no user and no reason behind it, like "Make me a fitness app." Quote the request. no if the prompt names who it is for or why.
Bad habit. Asks for a whole product or many features in one prompt with no steps or priorities. Quote the request. partly if it asks for a broad product in a few words.
Bad habit. A follow-up that only says to fix it or make it work, with no detail, like "Fix it." no if it says what to fix and how.
Bad habit. Accepts or ships AI output without checking it, like "ship whatever it generated". no if it asks to check or test.
